description_full: Maximus, Inc. provides tech-enabled services to government agencies in the United States and internationally. It operates through three segments: U.S. Federal Services, U.S. Services, and Outside the U.S. The company offers clinical services, including independent assessments of benefit eligibility; medical disability examinations; arbitration, appeals support, and payment resolution; eligibility and enrollment, outreach, and other services for federal health and human services programs; and technology solutions comprising automated systems and upgrades, and integration and management of disparate systems and processes. It also provides program operations, contact centers, clinical services, employment services, advanced technology solutions, and related professional services; Accuracy AssistantSM, an AI-enabled accuracy platform, and independent verification and validation services that provide independent technology oversight to help ensure systems meet requirements; specialized services, such as services to assist clients in procurement, business process assessment and design, implementation, quality assurance, policy and procedure reviews, and management of systems and projects; and cost allocation services, as well as audit assistance, and grant and proposal reviews. In addition, the company offers health and disability assessments, program administration for employment services, wellbeing solutions and other job seeker-related services, digitally-enabled customer services, and advanced technologies; employment services; and digitally enabled customer contact centers and services, and wellbeing solutions, as well as technology solutions, including health care administration software. It serves federal government, state and local government, and specialized markets. Maximus, Inc. was founded in 1975 and is based in McLean, Virginia.

financial_summary: Maximus, Inc. is a mid-cap industrials business with a $3.3B market cap on $5.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 13% against a 7% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 24% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $69M in free cash flow — roughly 1 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.29×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 2.0× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 6.7×.

Management returns a meaningful 8.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 12% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 550 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 26% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 7% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 37% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 37% and a beta of 0.64, it is more defensive than the market.
About $39.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 35% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 31% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 48% below its DCF fair value of $122, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 23%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $32.83 to $411 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Industrials peers: cheaper on P/E 9.3 vs 23.1 and EV/EBITDA 6.6 vs 13.3, richer on P/FCF 48.0 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 48% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 2.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 13.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $92.50 on average, 46% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 7.0%, but the 6pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.44).
It runs a 24% gross margin and converts 1% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.29x.
ROE of 21% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.7% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.0x net debt to EBITDA ($280.0M of cash against $1.6B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.7x.
Goodwill makes up 39% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.2% over 3 years, 4.2% over 5 years and 8.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 13.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -32.2% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.99 and a backlog worth 5% of annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 0.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 5, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.9%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 3 purchases and 1 sale over the past year, net $195K bought.
It returns 8.2% a year to shareholders (6.2% in buybacks and 2.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.2% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 21 consecutive years.
people: With about 33,700 employees, each generates about $155K of revenue, 0.4x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 12.2% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $2K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.3M (28x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
